en: They quickly finished saddling the horse,
Then laid on the bearskin crupper and white breastband
And had the straps drawn tight.
Leading the horse straight ahead,
They made him stride proudly,
Urging one another onward.
When the leopard mounted his horse,
They surged as though an enemy had come.
Clad imposingly in a golden coat,
He loomed like a white, rocky mountain;
His splendor appeared mountain-high
And captivated all who saw him.
Straining like a hungry lion,
The magnanimous hero rode forth,
Equipped with all his weapons.
At his side hung a scabbardless saber;
He took a spear with a steel shaft and sharp point,
Its blade a full handspan long.
Wondering what spectacle would unfold,
The gathered people lined the way.
Turning their faces toward Berish,
The chosen heroes rode forth.
Lest rain should soak it,
They loaded the white pavilion,
And many heroes secured it upon a camel.
The six horse-tending stewards,
All six equally valiant,
Set out with all the falcons,
Riding with longing toward the maiden.
Akjoltoy led the way,
His swift horse leaving only a streak,
As he left hills, ridges, and winding gullies
Far behind.
Akjoltoy, surging with vigor,
Led them onward.
Whenever they reached a suitable place,
They sported upon their tulpars,
And the restless heroes raced.
At other places
They grappled from the very hem,
And the reckless men seemed
Ready to destroy one another,
Until others seized their hands.
They charged, leveling spears,
And struck one another with whips.
Across countless hills and countless deserts,
They rode tirelessly onward.
Whenever they reached another place,
They began astonishing games.
They immersed themselves in sport,
Shooting when they saw wild asses,
Chasing gazelles and overtaking them,
And playing kök-börü,
Revealing the secrets in their hearts.
The treasures of their dear lives
They spent upon delight,
Immersing themselves in every pleasure
Until all their longings were eased.
As the heroes journeyed,
Across the boundless plain
They wrestled for the goat carcass from the ground.
They never traveled an ordinary journey,
But turned it into a hunt.
They plunged into immense,
Unending revelry.
They rode hard without sparing their horses
And raced in a sweeping free-for-all.
They crossed nameless mountain passes
And deserts no mortal had ever seen,
Beholding wondrous beasts—
Wild bulls and camel-like deer.
Upon the broad plain of Keng-Özön,
They camped in the pleasant valley,
And became guests of Keng-Özön.
Ah, wondrous Keng-Özön,
A valley blessed with perfect abundance.
If you ask what that valley was like,
Apples ripened until the boughs bent;
It was a land beloved by God.
Its springs boiled up and overflowed,
And nightingales sang mournfully.
When a sorrowful mortal heard
The nightingale’s voice, he wept.
Wild beasts inhabited the land,
Where no human being had ever come.
Even the bears had grown tame as cattle,
And its tigers bore twin cubs.
Wolves and foxes dwelt there,
Wild sheep streamed down the hills,
And every creature rejoiced.
Across the marshy islets,
Geese and ruddy shelducks mingled,
Calling loudly to one another.
They rejoiced at the sight of a human;
Who had ever seen such creatures?
Whoever saw them had every longing satisfied.
Great apes and butterflies
Filled its forests.
Ah, wondrous Keng-Özön,
A valley blessed with perfect abundance.
Is this not the finest of lands,
Where those who dwell never have their fill?
Its cow-parsnips are thick as an arm,
And when its startled deer bolt away,
They are like white-faced cows.
Its leaves are broad as hides,
Its currants large as thumbs,
Its lizards like snakes,
Its wild sheep like kulans.
Its ants are like greyhounds,
For Almighty God created
Wild beasts of every kind.
Lions, wildcats, tigers, and birds—
The grey-maned heroes’ day had dawned:
They stalked and shot the deer,
They shot and butchered the stags,
And the mighty men feasted
On bloody liver mixed with ashes.
The pleasure of roaming the hunt
Became a splendid pageant;
Such was the delight of the chase.
They remained there for six days,
Shooting bull deer and camel deer,
Bringing down every one of them;
Whenever a boar appeared before them,
They speared it through,
And reveled in abundant sport.
They took off their boots, stretched out their legs,
And slept soundly without stirring.
They remained carefree and untroubled,
Regarding bears and boars
As mere tusked enemies,
Not worth the hems of their robes.
Their bravery and lionhearted might
Almighty God in His power
Had bestowed without measure.
That noble hero, upheld by the spirits—
His fortune was complete.
He was a fortress with iron gates,
His wisdom broad as a river.
After Kuraaly and Kutubiy,
He was the hero born to surpass them.
When dawn began to glimmer,
And the cold wind before sunrise
Struck sharply against his face,
Then Akjoltoy
Awoke from his sweet sleep,
Rolled onto his right side,
And, unable to sleep, grew restless.
He stretched like a hungry lion,
And Joltoy rose from sleep.
He hurriedly performed his prayers,
Saddled Kulansur,
The steed with a kulan’s mane,
And without speaking many words,
His heart surging with joy,
He knew that the hapless peri-maiden
Had indeed arrived.
What had been foretold early had come late;
To behold the face
Of that hapless peri-maiden,
His two eyes became four with longing.
Accursed be mortal frailty:
His fly-sized soul cried out,
His heart surged and wandered,
The fire of love appeared before him,
And she seemed near to his eyes.
Your eagle-like kinsman Akjoltoy—
When he journeys, an army supports him,
A master of wisdom, a river of sense,
A seer who clearly knows
What is distant and what is near.
He is never trapped by the unknown;
Even in the moonless dark,
Once set upon a trail, he never strays.
His eyes can see afar;
When many gather for debate,
He alone emerges ahead in the contest.
He is the sage who unties the knots
Of every torment and tribulation.
He split a black hair exactly in two,
And seized his prize in an unguarded moment.
Against a fearsome enemy in adversity,
He attacked without retreating.
He was a marksman by ancestral inheritance,
A seasoned warrior looming like a mountain.
He was the wind-sheltered plane tree
Of grey-maned Sultan Seytek,
A lion-like champion who, once unleashed,
Let no living soul escape.
He would not let a white swan leave the lake,
That white-blazed black steed of a man.
Should a sudden flood sweep down,
He would stand unmoved and unshaken,
Never flinching from fear of the foe,
Standing beneath the battle standard.
When calamitous hardship came,
They would die in the same grave.
The reason they would die together was this:
They had sworn a solemn pledge
And bound it with utmost firmness.
They chewed white wheat flour together,
And licked the edge of steel;
Thus they swore their oath
And sealed their promise firmly.
They became friends until Judgment Day;
Seytek and Akjoltoy
Dwelt together as village neighbors,
Let alone the many campaigns stirred up from China.
In bravery and lionhearted might,
The names Akjoltoy and Seytek rang alike;
Two lion twins, two heroes—
How could either be lacking?
Against the foe they were vigilant,
On campaigns they were master marksmen,
Seasoned warriors worth the whole world.
On journeys their lives were one,
At pasture their livestock was one;
They shared their gathered wealth and treasure,
And if one died, the other prayed over him.
They shared the same feasts and companions,
Their villages and enclosures were one.
The marksman, brave Akjoltoy,
The noble hero, hurrying greatly,
Readied all his weapons,
Strapped on his gleaming sword,
For when had that hero ever held back?
He took up his ornamented gun,
Murmuring as his spirit rose,
Assuming many fearsome forms.
Kulunsur stood tethered there,
And Akjoltoy untied him,
In feverish haste.
Without setting foot in the gold-soled stirrup,
He sprang up in a single bound
And mounted Kulunsur.
Facing toward the north,
Your kinsman Joltoy rode away.
Beneath him, Kulunsur
Tore up the ground wherever he galloped;
When given his head, the furious steed
Thundered as though about to fly.
His tail filled an embrace, and he had a flowing mane;
The creature flew like a whirlwind.
His flanks were straight as a ramrod,
His compact frame small as a flea.
His poll was broad as a ewer,
And upon his croup one might set
A six-span cauldron with three supports
And leave it hanging there.
Akjoltoy’s Kulunsur
Was unlike any other beast.
The breadth between his forelegs
Was like a valley filled with meadowsweet.
The white blaze upon his brow
Was like polished steel.
